---
title: "How people actually use predictions"
editor:
  markdown:
    wrap: sentence
---

Everything in this course so far has been about producing a good number.
This page is about what happens after the number appears on someone's screen.

It deserves its own page because of a fact that is easy to state and easy to forget: **a model does not make decisions. A person does.**
A caseworker decides whether to open a case. A counselor decides whether to call a family. A supervisor decides whether to assign a slot.
The predicted probability is an input to that person's thinking, and how well the whole system works depends at least as much on that step as on your AUC.

A model with excellent performance, used badly, produces bad outcomes.
A model with modest performance, used thoughtfully, can genuinely help.

## Two ways it goes wrong

**People defer to the number too much.**
There is a well-documented tendency for people to trust output from a computer more than they trust their own judgment, even when they have information the computer does not.
This has a name --- *automation bias* --- and it is a problem because your model does not know that this family just moved in with a supportive grandmother, or that this student's attendance collapsed because of a temporary illness that has now resolved.
The staff member knows those things. If the score overrides them, the system has thrown away its best information.

**People ignore the number entirely.**
This is the more common failure, and it surprises people.
Staff who do not trust the tool, were not consulted about it, do not understand it, or find it inconvenient will simply work around it.
The scores get generated, nobody looks at them, and the organization believes it has a data-driven process when it does not.
This failure is quieter than the first one, because from the outside everything appears to be working.

Notice that these pull in opposite directions.
The goal is not to maximize how much staff follow the model, nor to minimize it.
It is for staff to weigh it appropriately --- and that depends on design choices, not on hoping.

## What the evidence looks like

The best-studied example in public services is the Allegheny Family Screening Tool, used in child welfare call screening in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania [@Allegheny2019].
Its design is worth knowing about because it is thoughtful, and the findings are genuinely mixed in an instructive way.

The tool produces a risk score, and for the very highest scores it triggers a protocol that defaults the referral toward being screened in for investigation.
Critically, **supervisors can override that default** --- they remain the decision-maker.

Two findings stand out.
First, supervisors used that authority substantially, overriding close to a quarter of the cases where the system defaulted to screening in.
They were not rubber-stamping.

Second, and more interesting: at one point a technical problem caused some scores to be badly miscalculated.
Workers turned out to be *more* likely to override the scores that were most wrong.
They were reading other information --- the referral itself, their own knowledge --- and noticing when the number did not fit.

That is genuinely encouraging.
It suggests human oversight can work rather than being a formality.
But it is a finding about one carefully designed system with trained supervisors, not a general guarantee, and the same body of research raises real concerns that risk scores can amplify existing bias by nudging staff toward "safe" decisions that fall unevenly across groups.
The lesson is not "humans will catch the errors." It is that oversight works when it is designed for and checked.

## Design choices that change behavior

These sound like small interface decisions. They are not.

-   **What you show.** A precise number ("0.73") invites more deference than a category ("elevated"), which invites more than a list of the factors involved. Showing *why* a case was flagged tends to produce better decisions than showing only *that* it was.

-   **What the default is.** A system where a high score automatically triggers an action, and a person must actively intervene to stop it, produces very different behavior from one where the score is advisory. Defaults are powerful.

-   **Whether overriding is easy or hard.** Requiring written justification to override creates a record and encourages thought --- and also discourages overriding, including when overriding is right. There is no setting that is free of trade-offs; choose deliberately.

-   **Whether staff know how accurate it is.** People calibrate their trust to what they are told. Staff who believe a tool is nearly always right will defer more than the evidence supports. Telling them plainly --- "of the people this flags, roughly one in three experience the outcome" --- helps them weigh it sensibly.

-   **Whether staff helped design it.** Tools that frontline staff were consulted on get used. Tools handed down do not. This is not only about buy-in: staff know things about the work that will improve the tool.

## Two things to watch after launch

**Track the humans, not just the model.**
Record how often staff override, in which direction, and --- importantly --- whether override patterns differ across demographic groups.
A perfectly fair model can produce unfair outcomes if staff systematically override it more for one group than another.
That is a bias pathway that never touches your model and would never appear in any of the metrics from the [bias section](bias_define.qmd).
It is invisible unless you deliberately look.

**Watch for feedback loops.**
This one is subtle and matters a great deal.
Once a model influences who receives a service, it starts shaping the data that future versions will be trained on.

Suppose the model flags certain students, those students receive extra attention, and the attention helps.
Next year's data now shows those students doing better --- and a model retrained on it may conclude they were never high risk.
Or the reverse: flagged families receive more scrutiny, more scrutiny produces more recorded incidents, and the next model learns that this kind of family really does have more incidents.
The model helped create the evidence for its own predictions.

There is no clean technical fix.
The defenses are awareness, keeping records of who was flagged and what was done, and --- best of all --- the kind of deliberate comparison group discussed in [designing deployments that let you learn](benefit_practice.qmd).
